Ojibways of Garden River First Nation

Garden River’s selected history follows the Shingwauk family’s educational aims and later community participation in land and highway negotiations. The sources offer distinct views of nineteenth-century pressures and a 1994 agreement process.

Read the sources [1] Shingwauk Residential Schools Centre [2] The Journal of Aboriginal Economic Development 3(2), 20–23; public copy at University of Saskatchewan I-Portal

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

The Shingwauk family’s educational vision

The Shingwauk Residential Schools Centre describes Shingwaukonse’s Teaching Wigwam vision as a place of shared learning and traces his family’s efforts to obtain educational resources. Its account also describes weakening government support, missionary changes and the growth of industrial schooling. Those changing colonial purposes matter when reading the family’s educational aims and the later institution’s history.

Read the sources [1] Shingwauk Residential Schools Centre

02

Member participation in land negotiations

In a 2003 article, negotiations coordinator Alice Corbiere describes Garden River’s 1994 land and highway agreements. The negotiating team opened meetings, distributed information to members living both on and away from the reserve, and arranged information sessions around work and family schedules. She credits communication and community inclusion in the referendum’s acceptance while noting that expectations about employment timing needed clearer explanation.

Read the sources [2] The Journal of Aboriginal Economic Development 3(2), 20–23; public copy at University of Saskatchewan I-Portal

Healing and Reconciliation Through Education — The Shingwauk Family and Early Mission Schools ↗

Publication: 2019

The archive’s educational history distinguishes the Shingwauk family’s educational vision from changing church and government policies. Its mission narrative requires attention to those differing purposes.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual chapters 7 and 8 read: Shingwauk family body (web lines 55–82) and early mission schools body (55–67). One work, two selected chapters.
